title: Learn with your AI
bullets: Use AI to understand AI. Then build something that helps you learn.
Week 6 · Learn, Vibe, Build · October 5, 2026
notes: 5:05–5:06. Teach through the slides first. One open-ended live conversation with Claude at the end, then small-group building. No predetermined build.

title: Your AI can help you learn about AI
bullets: Ask for an explanation at your level.
Ask it to quiz you, then explain what you missed.
Check its claims against the material you gave it.
notes: 5:06–5:08. Students can learn the tools by asking the tools. The answer is a starting point, not an authority.

title: This week’s reading: your AI as a coach
bullets: Arielle Shipper · How to Get Better at AI by Asking AI
Use examples of your own work to ask: “What should I learn next?”
Then: “Teach me that next step.”
notes: 5:08–5:10. Explicit tie: Shipper used her AI as a coach, reflecting on actual projects and learning the next step. Without long chat history, paste your last two submissions or describe what you have tried. The free reading link is in your account. No due date announced.

title: Markdown is just a text file
bullets: A .md file is plain text, with headings and lists.
You can read it. Your AI can read it.
A lesson or project context can live in that file.
notes: 5:10–5:12. # marks a heading; - marks a list. The lesson itself is markdown. No technical deep dive.

title: Context that sticks
bullets: Claude Code loads CLAUDE.md at session start.
Cursor and other coding tools can load AGENTS.md.
In a chat app: paste the file or add it to a Project.
notes: 5:12–5:14. Specific support varies by tool. These are ordinary files with plain words. They help the next session know what you mean without re-explaining everything. No live demo here and no template.

title: One small example
bullets: # Hill Plant Swap
A one-page website for a free plant swap near CU.
For first-year students who are nervous about going.
Keep it plain HTML and CSS. No JavaScript.
Use docs/event-facts.md. Never make up dates.
notes: 5:14–5:16. Read the example as what you would tell a new teammate. The point is persistent context, not a prescribed format.

title: A link someone else can open
bullets: file:// and localhost links only work on your computer.
A public HTTPS link works on someone else’s phone.
Commit → push → deploy are three different steps.
notes: 5:16–5:18. Commit saves a version locally. Push sends it to GitHub. Deploy publishes a website.

title: The short path online
bullets: GitHub Desktop: create repo → commit → publish.
GitHub: Settings → Pages → main / root → Save.
Open the published link on another phone.
notes: 5:18–5:20. Plain HTML/CSS: Pages. A framework app may need a different host such as Vercel. The handout is optional detail; all essential concepts are on this slide. No deployment demo tonight.

title: Next week: your AI reaches your tools
bullets: API: one program asking another for something.
Connector: your AI reaches tools directly, instead of you pasting.
This week we copy. Next week we’ll connect.
notes: 5:20–5:22. Concept only; no course connector, server address or setup.

title: Everything you need is on the Week 6 page
bullets: cu.learnvibe.build → Everything for Week 6
Click “Copy lesson as markdown” → paste into your AI.
Ask: “Teach me this and quiz me.”
notes: 5:22–5:25. Show where the button is without starting the demo yet. The lesson includes this invitation and enough context for the group work.

title: One live conversation with Claude
bullets: Copy the lesson markdown into Claude.
Talk through what you want to understand.
Maybe ask Claude to build a little thing from that conversation.
notes: 5:25–5:35. Aaron chooses the conversation and any build in the moment. No scripted project or staged before/after. If Claude stalls, discuss what you would ask and move into group work.

title: In small groups: build something that helps you learn
bullets: Choose your own topic and approach.
Try a quiz, interactive explainer, practice tool—or your own idea.
Use your AI, test what you build, and show what it helped you learn.
notes: 5:35 onward. This is the group-work invitation, not a rigid template. Students choose who to work with, what to learn and what to build. No predefined roles or prescribed file format.

title: Start with a learning question
bullets: What do you want to understand or practise?
Give your AI the lesson, your question, or both.
Build a small first version; try it and revise.
notes: Group work. Optional nudge: ask your AI what it needs to know about your project and save that context as markdown. If unsure where to start, use the Week 6 Copy button and ask for help choosing a learning idea. Work is not done merely because code runs: check whether it teaches the right thing.
